evidence_fragments.content:
Progressive Experience Fusion for Multi-Task World Model Control
in Endovascular Navigation
Harry Robertshaw 1, Maxence Boels 1, Nikola Fischer 1, Sebastien Ourselin 1, Christos Bergeles 1,
Alejandro Granados 1 and Thomas C Booth 1,2

The first phase
of MT has been split into five subtasks for multi-task RL
training, and is described in Fig. 2.

A ‘neck computed tomography angiography (CTA)’
scan of a stroke patient that encompassed the aortic arch to
the cerebral vessels, and a ‘body CTA’ scan encompassing
the abdominal and thoracic regions, including the femoral
arteries, descending aorta, and the aortic arch (obtained with
UK Research Ethics approval 24/LO/0057), were manually
processed into surface meshes, and arterial centerlines and
radii were extracted using 3D Slicer (v5.8.0) [35]. To fuse
the neck and body CTAs, the centerlines and radii of the ab-
dominal and thoracic regions were scaled so that the radius at
the most superior aspect of the descending aorta would match
the neck CTA aorta centerline. These two sets of centerlines
were joined, and the radius at each centerline point was used to
generate a surface mesh, which was loaded into the Simulation
Open Framework Architecture (SOFA, v23.12) [36]. This
process was repeated for 40 neck CTAs (which remained
unscaled), with the same body CTA scaled to fit each one

We use the same 10 patient
vasculatures for both training and testing as in previous
work, to first show that our proposed changes to TD-
MPC2 provide improvements over the current state-of-
the-art [33]. For training, five target locations in each
branch were used, and testing was performed on five
different targets per branch. ‘Test0’ refers to no unseen
vasculature.

20 randomly selected patient
vasculatures were then added to the Train10–Test0
dataset, to create a training set of 30. An additional
10 unseen patient vasculatures were used for testing
to evaluate generalization. Ten targets in each branch
were utilized for evaluation to comprehensively assess
performance across the entire branch.

This
utilizes the BeamAdapter plugin for SOFA, which was
used to model the vasculatures and the devices used for
navigation [37]. The devices modeled were a0.035”guidewire
(Terumo, Tokyo, Japan;120vertices with Young’s modu-
lus of43 MPa) and a0.0441”multipurpose (MP) catheter
(Terumo, Tokyo, Japan;160vertices with Young’s modulus
of47 MPa) [38].

No visual infor-
mation, including the geometry of the patient vasculature, was
available as observations during the navigation task. The target
location,p goal = (x′g, y′g), was resampled at the beginning of
each episode and remained fixed throughout that episode. At
time stept, the observation comprised the current and previous
device-position vectors,p t andp t−1, the target location, and
the previous action, as defined in (1).
ot = [pt,p t−1,p goal,a t−1](1)
The action vector contained the translation and rotation
speeds of both the guidewire and catheter. For each device,
the translational velocities were bounded to[−40,40] mm s −1,
and rotational velocities were bounded to[−180,180] ◦ s−1.

Two vascular phantoms
were printed: one geometry from Train10–Test0 and one
held-out geometry from Train30–Test10. Experiments were
conducted in a mock operating room. A mobile C-arm (Cios
Spin, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) was used
to provide fluoroscopic images as an input to a device tip-
tracking algorithm that extracted the necessary coordinates for
the state-based RL algorithm [40].

TD-MPC2 learns a compact latent world model
comprising an observation encoder, latent dynamics model,
reward predictor, ensemble of action-value functions, and
stochastic policy prior. At each control step, the current
observation is encoded into a latent state, after which candi-
date action sequences are evaluated by predicting their latent
trajectories, rewards, and terminal values.

Of theNcandidate sequences,N π are generated
by rolling out the learned policy prior, while the remaining
N−N π are sampled from the Gaussian proposal. All sampled
actions are bounded to the normalized action range. Each
candidate sequence is propagated through the latent dynamics
model and assigned the predicted return given by (3).

The evaluation, weighting, and proposal update in (3)–(5)
are repeated forKoptimization iterations. As high-return
action sequences become concentrated, the proposal standard
deviation (5) decreases, while a larger final standard deviation
indicates that the high-return action sequences remain more
dispersed. After the final iteration, an elite sequence is selected
according to the weights in (4). Only the first action is applied
to the environment, and planning is repeated after receiving
the next observation. The optimized proposal mean is shifted
forward by one step to initialize the following planning cycle.
We used the5×10 6-parameter TD-MPC2 configuration,
while increasing the replay-buffer capacity from1×10 6 to
1×10 7 transitions and the batch size from256to1024. An
LSTM-based observation embedder was additionally used to
integrate sequential device-tracking observations, allowing its
recurrent hidden state to retain information from the preceding
device-tip trajectory.

The adaptive signal is
interpreted as a measure of MPPI proposal concentration, not
as a direct measure of model uncertainty or procedural safety.

M2 = 1generalist agent that performs all navigation subtasks
across the corresponding vascular-anatomy distribution. The
layer sizes are(M 0, M1, M2) = (50,5,1)for Train10–Test0
(Nenv = 10) and(150,5,1)for Train30–Test10 (N env = 30).
Counting all layers, these configurations contain56and156
trained agent–buffer nodes, respectively.

To make use of this redundant transfer time, a patient-
specific simulator was constructed from the pre-operative
CTA, and a copy of the pretrained generalist agent underwent
time-bounded continued training through simulated interaction
before evaluation. No hyperparameters were changed during
the fine-tuning process. The reported fine-tuning times include
controller training only and exclude CTA segmentation, mesh
generation, simulation construction and data-transfer time.

Two
agents were fine-tuned from the PEF + adaptive horizon
model: one for a right-sided (A 1,A 2R,A 3R) and one
for a left-sided (A 1,A 2L,A 3L) navigation task.

Agents were allowed450exploration steps (equivalent to
approximately60s) duringin silicoevaluation. TheSuc-
cess Rate(SR) was defined as the percentage of evaluation
episodes in which the controller successfully reaches the
target; for unsuccessful episodes,Path Ratio(PR) was defined
as100(d 0 −d T )/d0, whered 0 andd T are the initial and final
centreline distances to the target, respectively; andProcedure
Time(PT) was defined as the time taken from the start of
navigation to the target location for successful episodes [46].
Each evaluation step recorded the SR, PT, and PR. For the
model with the highest SR, the corresponding PR and PT were
examined.

In vitrotesting was conducted in a mock operating room
where each subtask was carried out five times for each agent,
recording the SR, PT, and PR. Forin vitroevaluation of the
Train30–Test10 dataset, theA 2L subtask was split into two
measures of success due to its difficulty [33], as shown in
Fig. 6. The first was navigating the guidewire inside of the
LCCA branch to any degree (A 2L -lower branch), while the
second was to navigate further up the LCCA to the original
target (A 2L -upper branch, whereby the guidewire provides
a stable base for the catheter to follow). Agents were allowed
5 minduringin vitroevaluation, to account for the speed of
the robotic manipulator.
Comparative statistical analyses were conducted using two-
sided independent-samples Student’st-tests, with statistical
significance defined asp <0.05, for bothin silicoandin
vitroexperiments.
SAC and base TD-MPC2 results taken from [33].

Overall, PEF achieved a mean SR of 74% with improved
performance compared to SAC (37%,p <0.001), and a trend
for improved performance compared to base TD-MPC2 (65%,
p= 0.053).

PEF
achieved a mean SR of 73% with a trend for improved per-
formance compared to SAC (50%,p= 0.069); and a similar
performance compared to base TD-MPC2 (63%,p= 0.414),
with comparable PTs to base TD-MPC2.

The baseline PEF achieved a mean SR of
89%, a mean PR of69%, and a mean PT of20.6 s. Utilizing
ouradaptive horizonmethod with PEF gave a similar mean SR
of90%(p= 0.719) with an improved PR of78%(p <0.001),
and a similar mean PT of19.5 s(p= 0.416).

with PR increasing from69%
to78%(p= 0.031).

Duringin silicofine-tuning, training speeds were calculated
to be≈6.21 steps/s, meaning20×10 3 fine-tuning steps were
equivalent to≈54 min.

SAC and base TD-MPC2 results taken from previous work, but updated
for the splitting of theA 2L task [45].

Based
on the results of Section III-D, the40×10 3 fine-tuning step
model was used for comparison during evaluation. Fine-tuning
gave a mean SR of67%compared to60%without fine-tuning
(p= 0.623). Mean PR improved from63%to80%with fine-
tuning (p <0.001), while mean PT did not appear to be
compromised.

shows fluoroscopic images of a successfulin vitronavigation
attempt ofA 2R, and an unsuccessful navigation ofA 2R due

Gains in performance became non-monotonic after approxi-
mately40×10 3 fine-tuning steps, which equates to107 min
and so is within a real-world inter-hospital transfer window,
and is close to the CT-to-puncture window in MT-capable
hospitals where patients are not transferred. All fine-tuning
experiments were performed on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU,
and the reported times reflect this computational setup.

The present
results establish proof of concept for fluoroscopy-guided
transfer to one held-out patient-derived geometry.

legacy_cells.B: Progressive Experience Fusion for Multi-Task World Model Control in Endovascular Navigation
legacy_cells.C: Robertshaw, Harry, Boels, Maxence, Fischer, Nikola, Ourselin, Sebastien, Bergeles, Christos, Granados, Alejandro, et al.
legacy_cells.J: Primary method – application/adaptation of existing WM
legacy_cells.O: Acute ischemic stroke requiring mechanical thrombectomy
legacy_cells.S: Can one TD-MPC2-based controller navigate multiple endovascular thrombectomy subtasks across vascular anatomies and transfer to a held-out patient-derived in-vitro vasculature?
legacy_cells.U: General interventionalists are discussed as the intended users of AI-assisted robotic thrombectomy navigation.
legacy_cells.V: Navigate a guide catheter and guidewire to a selected vascular target.
legacy_cells.AI: 2D coordinates of three device-tip tracking points, target location, previous device positions, and previous action
legacy_cells.AJ: TD-MPC2 observation encoder with an LSTM-based observation embedder for sequential device-tracking observations
legacy_cells.BD: Guidewire and catheter translation and rotation speeds. Translation bounds are −40 to 40 mm s−1 and rotation bounds are −180 to 180° s−1.
legacy_cells.BI: Progressive Experience Fusion (PEF) multi-task controller using TD-MPC2
legacy_cells.BU: Dense reward: −0.00015 − 0.001 × change in centerline pathlength, plus 1 when the target is reached. MPPI return also includes a terminal Q-value.
legacy_cells.CI: Base planning horizon is 3 steps and is extended adaptively from final MPPI proposal dispersion. Numeric Hmax is not reported.
legacy_cells.CK: MPPI maximizes predicted discounted rewards plus terminal Q-value. Reward penalizes centerline pathlength increase and adds 1 on target reach. Actions are bounded to the normalized action range.
legacy_cells.DB: N/A for the single generalist controller used at runtime
legacy_cells.DC: LSTM recurrent hidden state retains information from the preceding device-tip trajectory.
legacy_cells.DN: Train10–Test0 and Train30–Test10 datasets of patient vasculatures
legacy_cells.EC: Decision/control performance: on Train10–Test0 in silico, PEF mean success rate 74%, versus 37% for SAC and 65% for base TD-MPC2. On Train30–Test10, PEF plus adaptive horizon achieved 90% mean success rate and 78% path ratio. On one unseen in-vitro vasculature, 40 × 10³ fine-tuning steps improved mean path ratio from 63% to 80%.
legacy_cells.EG: Fine-tuning speed was approximately 6.21 steps/s. 40 × 10³ fine-tuning steps corresponded to approximately 107 min in the reported patient-specific adaptation experiment.
legacy_cells.EI: Soft Actor-Critic baseline: in Train10–Test0 in-silico evaluation, mean success rate 37% versus PEF 74% (p < 0.001).
legacy_cells.EJ: Base TD-MPC2 baseline: in Train10–Test0 in-silico evaluation, mean success rate 65% versus PEF 74% (p = 0.053).
legacy_cells.EK: Compared PEF with and without adaptive horizon. On Train30–Test10, mean success rate was 89% versus 90%, while mean path ratio was 69% versus 78%.
legacy_cells.EL: Unsuccessful navigation included catheterization of the brachiocephalic artery or right subclavian artery. Discussion identifies failure to provide a stable catheter base as a barrier in the difficult A2L task.
legacy_cells.ER: UK Research Ethics approval 24/LO/0057 is reported for the CTA data.
legacy_cells.FB: Compact continuous latent state encodes observations and latent dynamics for action-sequence prediction, reward prediction, and control.
legacy_cells.FL: Tracking coordinates, target, and previous action are encoded into a latent state. TD-MPC2 latent dynamics, reward predictor, action-value functions, and policy prior score candidate action sequences in MPPI. Only the first action is executed before a new observation and replanning. PEF fuses replay experience across anatomy and navigation-task layers. In vitro, fluoroscopic tracking feeds the state-based controller and a robotic manipulator executes catheter and guidewire motions.
legacy_cells.FM: Introduces Progressive Experience Fusion to train a multi-task TD-MPC2 controller across anatomy and navigation subtasks, an adaptive MPPI horizon based on residual action-proposal dispersion, and patient-specific fine-tuning. Evaluates in-silico generalization and transfer to an unseen in-vitro vasculature.
legacy_cells.FN: PEF achieved 74% mean success in Train10–Test0 in silico versus 37% for SAC and 65% for base TD-MPC2. On 10 held-out anatomies, PEF with adaptive horizon achieved 90% mean success and 78% path ratio. In one unseen in-vitro anatomy, fine-tuning improved mean path ratio from 63% to 80%.
legacy_cells.FO: Only two device types were used. Only one unseen in-vitro phantom was evaluated. The authors call for evaluation across more unseen anatomies and ex-vivo and in-vivo modalities. The phantom lacked vessel compliance and pulsatility. Scalability beyond the two task dimensions evaluated remains unestablished.
legacy_cells.FP: Evaluate scalability to full mechanical-thrombectomy navigation and additional clinical variations, assess further horizon-adaptation strategies and broader RL tasks, test more unseen in-vitro anatomies before ex-vivo and in-vivo work, and investigate dual tracking or image-based reinforcement learning to improve catheter use and stability.
legacy_cells.FQ: Prior endovascular navigation work had not tested unseen vasculature in vitro with a multi-task world-model controller; cited TD-MPC2 navigation work was limited to known anatomy and in-silico evaluation.
legacy_cells.FR: Evidence is a technical proof of concept in simulation and vascular phantoms, including one unseen in-vitro anatomy. It does not establish clinical efficacy, prospective patient benefit, full-procedure autonomy, in-vivo safety, or causally identified treatment effects. Adaptive action-proposal dispersion is not a validated estimate of model uncertainty or procedural safety.

limitations: Automated model review, not independent human verification, replication or clinical validation.

This synthesis considered all twelve supplied text pages and all earlier page/image-review notes, but received no page images directly. Direct image inspection is attributable only to the documented earlier API calls.
Chunk-local notes about unavailable other page ranges are superseded by the combined packet. No missing-page limitation is inferred for this synthesis.
Source hash, path and prior API receipts are supplied provenance, not independently recomputed or verified filesystem facts.
No executable schema/source/semantic validator, graph rebuild, file write or canonical admission was performed.
All 46 printed references were considered as bibliography content; their full texts were not retrieved. Cited systems' capabilities are not inherited.

Core procedural world-model implementation and model-coupled control support L4 independently of missing separate successor-fidelity, matched alternative-action prediction, calibration and effective-horizon tests.
Model identifiers denote reported configurations, not exact seeds/weights/checkpoints. The adapted identifier is a provisional condition group including side-specific copies.

The LSTM observation embedder is not necessarily the dynamics backbone. Transition layers, losses, multi-step gradient behavior and value-equivalence objectives cannot be imported from a TD-MPC2 citation.
The 5×10^6-parameter TD-MPC2 configuration is not a verified total including the added LSTM.
Numerical adaptive alpha/Hmax, several MPPI settings, recurrent reset/context rules, exact command cadence, normalization and coordinate frames are incomplete.
Proposal dispersion is explicitly not model uncertainty or procedural safety; it establishes neither calibration nor support/hazard detection.
PEF transfers post-training replay and retrains agents. It does not establish neural parameter fusion, a runtime hierarchy, multiscale dynamics or inference-time utility substitution.
Replay balancing, overflow/eviction, deduplication, sampling, higher-layer weight initialization and matched total training compute are unclear.
Forty environments reuse one body CTA; they are not forty independently acquired full femoral-to-cerebral anatomies. Unique participant counts cannot be inferred by adding scan counts.

Known-anatomy target holdout and held-out-anatomy simulation are distinct. Human-derived CTA geometry does not convert simulated/phantom navigation into qualifying held-out actual clinical validation for R2.
Only two physical geometries, including one unseen phantom, were studied. Five repetitions per task are not independent anatomies; lower/upper A2L outcomes may be dependent.
Adapted testing follows exposure to the anatomy-specific simulator and is not untouched zero-shot anatomy evaluation.
PR describes failures and PT successes. Changing conditional subsets and unclear mean weighting limit unconditional and cross-condition comparisons.
The meaning of ±, seed counts, allocation across episodes/anatomies, clustering, pairing, multiplicity and checkpoint/final-test independence are incompletely documented.
Nonsignificance does not demonstrate equivalence, noninferiority or no effect.
Adaptive A2L PR is 78% in prose and 79±13% in Table III. Both are retained; aggregate PR 78±12% is a separate endpoint.
The adaptation series starting at 41% SR concerns one simulated anatomy and differs from the ten-anatomy aggregate at 90%; these are not established contradictory measurements.

Reported 107-min adaptation time excludes segmentation, mesh/simulator construction and data transfer, and exceeds the cited approximately 90-min local CT-to-puncture interval. Compatibility with a cited approximately 190-min transfer interval is not validated clinical workflow feasibility.
Training steps, MPPI iterations, control steps, navigation duration and clinical time are distinct coordinates.

Wrong-branch navigation, persistent A2L-upper failure and non-monotonic adaptation are reported. Vessel injury, force, radiation exposure, perforation/dissection and comprehensive safe-failure endpoints are not established.
PEF is not uniformly superior: Table I A2L SR is 8% versus base TD-MPC2 22%; aggregate PEF procedure time is longer. Aggregate adaptive-horizon and adapted-phantom SR differences are nonsignificant.
First-in-field, superhuman and device-stability explanations are author claims/interpretations, not independent priority verification, expert-comparator results or causal isolation experiments.
Historical baseline reuse links B049 to [33]/B105 and [45]/B051; repeated reporting is not independent corroboration.
Named ethics approval is not product authorization. Its parenthesis attaches to body CTA; all-neck-CTA coverage and consent arrangements remain unclear.
Only R1 is supported. Human/expert review, prospective patient/workflow use, comparative clinical benefit and authorized monitored deployment are unestablished.
Full thrombectomy, clot retrieval, stent deployment, higher-dimensional fusion and ex-vivo/in-vivo extensions remain future work.
